paragraphs: The windows of the Secretariat’s western storeroom had not been opened in years.

It had once housed ritual vessels, and the doors still carried greenish traces where bronze locks had worn against them. At the end of spring the vessels were moved out, and high shelves on every wall filled with old registers from Guanzhong, household records of the former Yan from Ye, and paper scrolls from the garrisons of Hexi. The edges of the hemp paper were rough with windblown sand; some cords around the old Xianbei files had rotted through. Night rain came through the tiles. Clerks threw worn felt over the shelves until their own shoulders and backs were soaked.

The youngest clerk was Lu Xun, newly assigned to the Revenue Office and still unable to distinguish all the seals of three successive courts. One day he found three registers that appeared unrelated. The first listed Li Acheng, a Han household from Shiping; the second named Li Cheng of the Left Army, an attached soldier of a Di camp; the third recorded only Acheng, a fugitive household member with no known village. Their ages differed by a year or two, but in all three the wife was named A-Yun, and the son’s childhood name was the same.
“Master,” Lu Xun called to the elderly keeper of the records, “are these three people, or one?”
The old clerk bent over the lamp, brushed dust from a register with his fingertip, and finally said, “Ask the offices below us. Who issued him his grain?”
“The old military office says his unit has been dissolved. Shiping says he fled labor service. The fugitive-household register says his whereabouts are unknown.”
“Are they still collecting taxes from him?”
“All three have him in their arrears ledgers.”
The old clerk turned up the lamp and sighed. “He passed through three places and came to owe grain to all three. If he returns asking for one mu of land, not one of them will acknowledge him.”

Lu Xun said nothing. He found a discarded list of ritual offerings and copied the old registration, present residence, and army enrollment onto one sheet, which he laid across the three scrolls with a length of hemp cord. His handwriting was poor, but it saved two rounds of searching. The old man did not scold him. He said only, “Keep the old scrolls. Don’t let your handwriting erase the first half of a man’s life.”

Fu Hong saw this composite sheet in the western storeroom after the murder of Gao Yunde in Hedong. Land disputes reached the Secretariat every day. Wives separated from their soldier husbands could not find the household registrations of their husbands' families. Refugees sheltered by great estates were taxed in two places. Several Qiang veterans knew only their tribes' old names, while county clerks insisted that they write down the ancestral home of their family. Even after a surveyor had established every field boundary, there was often no one the office could identify as the lawful recipient of the land.

Lu Xun thought the Crown Prince had come to accuse him of privately altering official records and immediately prostrated himself. Fu Hong told him to rise. “How do you know these three scrolls describe one man?”
“Lady A-Yun came to the military office last year seeking the death benefit. She brought a wooden token.”
“Where is it?”
“I was afraid it would get lost, so I sewed it to the back of this old ritual list.”

At Fu Hong’s order they undid the stitches. The token was indeed carved with an old military unit number. On its reverse was a tiny character for Yun, almost rubbed away. Years of travel lay within that small piece of wood.

Fu Hong then had the attached notes from Hedong and Ye brought in. Clerks in other places, he discovered, were already using similar clumsy remedies under different names. He did not issue an edict at once. He spread seven or eight kinds of composite sheets across a long table and asked the old keeper to explain where each was most likely to go wrong. Then he ordered three counties to conduct trials. The original registers were to be kept intact; the new sheets would show only current residence, kinship ties, and holdings awaiting verification. Any summons for labor service still had to be checked against the old records.

Before a month of trial had passed, a complaint arrived from Hedong. A military household had received a work summons from the old army office in the morning and another from the new composite sheet in the afternoon. Only two teenage boys remained in the home, yet on the same day each had been ordered to a different irrigation canal. Lu Xun sat all night with the erroneous orders in his hands. The next morning he carried the file to Fu Hong and confessed his fault.

A widow from the commandery submitted a petition for her son, who was still too young for conscript labor. The old camp had nevertheless called him into service under his dead father’s military enrollment. Fearful that the clerks would confuse their documents, she had tied her late husband’s lacquered wooden badge to the boy’s household slip with hemp thread. Lu Xun dared not grant an exemption on the spot and told her to wait in the county lodging. That night, when he tracked down the child’s name, he discovered that officials in another county had copied it down as if it belonged to his father.
“Have you brought him home?” the Crown Prince asked.
“Yes. But the other county refuses to cancel the summons. They say the new sheet bears the Secretariat’s seal.”

Fu Hong circled the two dates on the mistaken orders. “Exempt him this time. Find out who issued them in error and record the fault according to the regulations. If these new pages cannot yet save people a journey, don’t rush to send them through the commanderies.”

The trials stopped for three days. Lu Xun took his clerks down to the counties and compared the supporting slips one by one, identifying several kinds of mistakes involving miscopied names, identical names, and false declarations. When the trials resumed, he left a small space at the top of each composite sheet for the words “date of reverification.” The old keeper looked at it and smiled. “A person’s days go forward. Paper ought to have a date it can answer for as well.”

Composite sheets from the provinces filled half a room. Someone copying them casually wrote “Qin sheets” on a packing case; by the time the case reached the Secretariat, someone else had changed the label to “Qin registers.” The name existed before the rules were complete. Di nobles who had won honors in battle resisted being checked alongside newly submitted soldiers; the great families of Ye feared having their pedigree entered on a common page; Qiang chiefs worried that officials from Chang’an would bypass them and reach directly into each household. In the storeroom Lu Xun heard only the urgent demands for files. He did not know how fiercely those two characters were being contested outside.
That autumn, a dispute over the inheritance of a military land grant came from Weichang County.

The dead commander Helai Zhen had served in the old Former Yan army. After submitting to Qin he campaigned in Hexi and fought in the north beyond the passes, dying in camp three years earlier. His military merit had earned him eighty mu of land, a house, and six horses. His son A-Luo was ten. The child’s mother, Lady Zhao, came from a Han refugee family; she had neither a formal marriage document nor a place in the Helai clan genealogy. While alive, Helai Zhen had entered his wife and son in the army’s family register. After his death the clan denied the boy’s right to inherit the fields and drove away five of the horses. Lady Zhao took her son back to her own relatives, but the Zhao family, afraid of offending the Xianbei clan elder, said the child belonged to another surname.

The Weichang magistrate placed the eighty mu under seal and allowed the dispute to drag through two whole planting seasons. When Lady Zhao came to the county office for millet seed, the clerk asked which family she belonged to. She went home, cut the cuffs from an old robe left by Helai Zhen, and made it into an autumn coat for A-Luo. That night she sat by lamplight mending the seams, not once allowing herself to cry aloud.
When the case came to Chang’an, Fu Hong summoned the disputants to the Secretariat.

The Helai clan elder carried an old saber in his arms. Nearly seventy, he spoke with the accent of Yan. He entered the hall and laid the weapon on the mat before saying that Helai Zhen had mounted a horse at twelve, equipped with horses, armor, and bows supplied by his clan. The clan could not simply surrender to outsiders the honor it had guarded for generations.
Fu Hong asked, “Who gave birth to the boy?”
“The Zhao woman.”
“Did his father acknowledge him?”
“He did.”
“Then what is there left to dispute?”

The old man’s eyes rested on the scabbard. “General, much is never written in official registers. Within our clan, the order of carrying the ancestral sword at sacrifice follows seniority. If land passed down from our forebears goes to someone never presented at the rites, who will still provide horses for the clan?”
Lady Zhao had kept her head lowered. Now she suddenly took from her sleeve a small faded saddle, its leather straps too short to fit anything larger than a sheep.

“When A-Luo was a month old, the clan brought him a little horse. At seven, when he learned to ride, his great-uncle held the reins. On the day Helai Zhen received his land, all his uncles came to our house to drink. Everyone said then that this boy would one day look after those eighty mu.”
She set the little saddle beside the saber and said quietly, “Now that his father is dead, does even the wine you drank that day count for nothing?”
The elder’s eyelids twitched. He stroked the hilt but gave no answer.

By the time Fu Jian approached the hearing, the county magistrate’s knees had gone numb from kneeling. The Crown Prince presented the army enrollment and compensation rolls, and father and son read them together. Helai Zhen, deputy commander of the Qin army. Son: A-Luo. Wife: Zhao. The writing was not recent, and the old seal was genuine. Fu Jian asked the child, “What did your father teach you?”
“To ride. He taught me to see the colors of the grass first. A hole hidden in grass can break a horse’s leg.”
“Anything else?”
“He wanted me to grow the fields well. He said then I wouldn’t have to spend my whole life going to war with other people.”

Fu Jian set the register down and first asked the elder whose saber it was. The elder said it was an old Helai family weapon, lent to Helai Zhen for his campaigns. Fu Jian nodded. “The saber remains yours. As for sacrifices and the old genealogy, follow your clan’s customs.”
Some of the tension left the elder’s shoulders. Then Fu Jian pointed to the written grant of military farmland.

“These eighty mu were not allotted by your clan. The Qin army granted them for Helai Zhen’s service. The government cannot let the name of his son disappear from the military register merely because the father has died.”
“Your Majesty,” the clan elder protested, “what if the boy refuses to acknowledge the Helai family when he grows up?”

“He acknowledges it today.” Fu Jian turned to A-Luo. “What happens later is for you living people to settle among yourselves. For now, the fields go to him under the original grant. If the irrigation canal or horse pasture is shared with the clan and ownership is disputed, that must be heard separately. No one is to use this ruling to throw other people out.”
“And the horses?” A-Luo asked.

The elder said five were still alive; one had died of sickness the year before last. Fu Jian ordered the county officials to inspect the animals and assess their value: the living horses must be returned and compensation paid for the dead one at its market value at the time. The old man was not to be forced to produce the money there in the hall. Though A-Luo had heard the fields were his, he kept looking at the saber. The elder lifted it and rose to go, but stopped abruptly in front of the child.
“When your father first wore this, he stood a whole head taller than you do now.”
The boy said nothing.
“Look after the fields he left you. When you can draw his bow, come to the ancestral shrine.”

The old man went out with the saber in his arms and did not look back. Lady Zhao did not follow him. She asked the county clerk only when the canal water would reach the eighty mu in Weichang that year. In the hall they had disputed bloodlines. Now she needed to know whether the spring fields could be sown.

In the western storeroom Lu Xun copied A-Luo’s composite sheet. It took him three tries to enter the field number, his father’s military grant, and his mother’s present county of residence correctly. He removed nothing from the old registers; beside the new entry he wrote the judgment and the name of the official responsible for reverification. When he smoothed the page down, the added layer of paper was almost too thin to see.

Two months later the reports came back from the three trial counties. Some people had been spared journeys, while others had been entered under the wrong village. Mistaken sheets still had to be checked against the original scrolls, and double conscriptions or false names could not be made to vanish by writing on a new page. Only then did the Secretariat promulgate preliminary rules for combined verification, with time allowed for corrections in each commandery. County officials could use the new register to allot land, collect grain, and verify compensation, but matters involving old clan property or marriage customs still required the supporting original deeds.

Tender shoots of winter wheat were already growing in Weichang. At the edge of the fields, an inspector saw a new boundary post leaning as if someone had kicked it in the night. Lady Zhao was righting it, while A-Luo crouched at the canal inlet with a gourd dipper. Some boys from the clan passed in the distance and still called him “the Han woman’s brat.” He clenched his teeth and said nothing. Only when they were gone did he ask his mother why his father had never entered his name in the genealogy.
Lady Zhao watched the canal water run toward the field. “I suppose he thought he would come home.”

The boy was silent for a while. Then he stood and placed the dipper back into the furrow. The inspector stamped his seal on the thin register, entering once more the rightful owner of eighty mu. On his way back to the county town, he heard A-Luo calling to an ox behind him. The voice was still boyishly high, yet already carried a trace of the accent of his father’s old army.
